title: Dre Greenlaw ejection: What NFL officials said about 49ers LB
description: San Francisco 49ers linebacker Dre Greenlaw was ejected from the team's game vs. the Seattle Seahawks. The officials explained why after the game.
fullText:
It looked like a devastating blow for the San Francisco 49ers defense Sunday when linebacker Dre Greenlaw was ejected in the second quarter.

Greenlaw with 6:30 to go was flagged for hitting Seattle Seahawks quarterback Sam Darnold after he went out of bounds. It was a close play, but one Greenlaw probably could've avoided and one that is certainly worthy of a personal foul penalty under the NFL rules. What happened after was something that can't happen.

After the play in a scuffle on the Seattle sideline, Greenlaw headbutted Seahawks linebacker Ernest Jones who was not wearing a helmet. It was the kind of action that's going to get a player ejected, and Vice President of Instant Replay Mark Butterworth confirmed to ESPN's Brady Henderson after the game why Greenlaw was disqualified.

"The clubs passed a rule this year that the AMGC (Art McNally Gameday Central in New York) can actually eject a player even when there is not a flag down on the field for the action," Butterworth told Henderson. "But in this case, there was a flag down on the field. When they went to the sideline, the player in question actually head-butted a non-helmeted player on the sideline. We have a very specific process we go through. (NFL Executive Vice President of Football Operations) Troy Vincent let us know that the player was ejected, so then I communicated with the field to inform them that number 57 was ejected from the game for a non-football act. "

That's about as straightforward as it gets.

Even in a heat-of-the-moment scenario, a player wearing a helmet can't do something as dangerous as headbutting a player not wearing a helmet. The act didn't injure Jones in any way, but it certainly could have which is why the league isn't going to let a player get away with it.

San Francisco's defense recovered from the loss of their tone-setting linebacker. They won't want to play many more games without him, though, so ideally Greenlaw won't receive any additional suspension or have this sort of in-game issue again.

title: Claude-Pod
description: Docker sandbox for the Claude Code CLI. Runs Claude against one project folder — including with --dangerously-skip-permissions — while your home directory, SSH keys, and other projects stay invisib...
fullText:
Docker sandbox for the Claude Code CLI. Runs Claude against one project folder — including with --dangerously-skip-permissions — while your home directory, SSH keys, and other projects stay invisible to the container. Unofficial.

claude-pod runs Claude Code inside a Docker container that mounts the project folder you launch it from. Claude can read and edit that folder; the rest of your machine — home directory, SSH keys, other projects, host shell — isn't mounted, so the container can't see it.

It's not full isolation — here's the boundary:

The practical effect: the worst case is narrowed from "your whole machine" to "this one folder," which is recoverable from git.

Docker is the only requirement — no Node.js, npm, or claude needed on your host. For the full threat model and the four-file design, see Security and limits. For the official approach, see Anthropic's Claude Code sandboxing documentation.

Just Docker. Claude Code runs inside the container, not on your host — you do not need Node.js, npm, or the claude CLI installed on your machine. The host stays untouched apart from one state folder (~/.claude-pod/) that exists only to keep your login across container restarts.

Call the script using its full or relative path from any project:

You land in a bash shell at the same path your project lives at on the host (e.g. /Users/you/projects/anything), with claude on PATH. Run it however you like:

Alternatively, you may skip the shell and go straight into Claude. Anything you pass to claude-pod is run inside the container instead of bash. So this drops you directly into Claude in one command, and exits the container when Claude exits:

Forgot a command later? Run ~/tools/claude-pod/claude-pod --help (or -h) anytime — it prints a copy-pastable cheatsheet of every command (run, install, update, uninstall, options), with the correct absolute paths for your install.

For your convenience, you can add an alias to your shell configuration file (~/.zshrc, ~/.bashrc, etc.):

This is the shell-first form: claude-pod drops you into the container with claude on PATH, so you can run npm install, a dev server, or tests and then start claude yourself — all inside the sandbox. The same alias also goes straight into Claude when you pass the command through: claude-pod claude --dangerously-skip-permissions.

The first time you start Claude inside the pod, it will print a login URL. Open it in your host browser, complete the login, paste the verification code back into the container, and you're done. The session persists in ~/.claude-pod/ and survives container restarts — you only do this once per machine.

Bind your dev server to 0.0.0.0 inside the container, not localhost. Most dev servers default to localhost, which means they only listen on the container's own loopback — your host browser can't reach them even with PORTS=... set. Common fixes:

The host-side mapping is still 127.0.0.1-only (forced by claude-pod), so binding 0.0.0.0 inside the container does not expose your dev server to your LAN.

Claude can only read files that live inside the project folder — that's the one directory bind-mounted into the container. Images on your Desktop or in Downloads aren't mounted, so pasting one straight from there hands Claude a path it can't reach. This is the same isolation that keeps the rest of your machine private from the container (What is and isn't isolated); the small bit of friction below is the price for not exposing those default locations.

To pin a specific version, set CLAUDE_CODE_VERSION:

Pinned versions cache normally across rebuilds. The script prints the resolved version after each build, so you always know what you got.

The image is intentionally minimal: node:24-slim + git + curl + less + jq + gh + Claude Code. Nothing language-specific. Anything your projects need (Python, build tools, other toolchains) you add yourself — edit the Dockerfile and re-run ~/tools/claude-pod/install.sh.

The whole tool is four tiny files:

Where Claude can actually write — two paths, both intentional bind mounts:

Because the current directory ($PWD) is mounted into the container, avoid running this tool from directories like root (/) or /etc or other sensitive ones. In such cases you are giving the AI access to your entire machine or to other sensitive data, defeating the purpose of the sandbox. Always cd into your specific project folder first.

Everywhere else Claude writes is either in the container's ephemeral filesystem (discarded on exit thanks to --rm) or simply has no path to land at — the Linux kernel's mount namespace makes any other host directory invisible to the container. Symlinks inside the project folder pointing to ~/.ssh or /etc/passwd appear broken for the same reason: those targets aren't mounted, so the container can't see them.

Hardlinks are different. A hardlink is a second name for an existing inode on the same filesystem. If a file inside your project folder is hardlinked to a sensitive file elsewhere on the same filesystem (e.g., ~/.ssh/id_rsa), the container can reach it through the hardlink — the bind-mount exposes the inode, not just the path. This requires the hardlink to already exist in the project folder, so it's a real concern only when you're inspecting code from an untrusted source. Treat unfamiliar projects with the same caution you'd apply to running their code directly: don't run claude-pod inside a folder you don't trust.

The tradeoff: the worst case becomes "something bad happens to one project folder," which is recoverable from git, instead of "my entire home directory is exposed."

NET=none and PORTS are mutually exclusive — a container with no network can't publish ports. --pids-limit is always applied (it contains fork bombs, which dropped capabilities do not prevent); raise PIDS= if a very parallel build hits the ceiling.

Everything this repo causes to exist outside the project you launch it from:

No sudo, no writes to /usr/local/, /etc/, ~/.zshrc, ~/Library/, your existing ~/.claude/, or anywhere else on the host.

The wrapper is portable POSIX bash + Docker. It should work on any host with a recent Docker:

Native Windows (cmd.exe / PowerShell) is not supported. The wrapper is a bash script and uses POSIX tools (id, etc.); use WSL2 instead.

If a platform doesn't behave as expected, please open an issue.

Removes ~/.claude-pod/ and the claude-pod image after confirmation. Tells you exactly what it isn't touching (node:24-slim, build cache, this repo) and how to clean those up yourself.

If you added a shell alias for convenience (e.g. alias claude-pod=... in ~/.zshrc / ~/.bashrc), remove that line too — uninstall.sh doesn't touch your shell rc files.

title: Brewers ace Jacob Misiorowski labors into 5th inning of NLCS opener against Dodgers
description: — It was a really challenging night for Milwaukee Brewers ace Jacob Misiorowski.The front-runner for the NL Cy Young Award labored just to make it to the fifth inning of the NL Championship Series opener against the Los Angeles Dodgers on Sunday night.
fullText:
MILWAUKEE (AP) — It was a really challenging night for Milwaukee Brewers ace Jacob Misiorowski.

The front-runner for the NL Cy Young Award labored just to make it to the fifth inning of the NL Championship Series opener against the Los Angeles Dodgers on Sunday night.

Los Angeles fouled off 21 of his 94 pitches by the time his final batter, Mookie Betts, reached on a one-out walk in the fifth. The 24-year-old allowed one run and five hits.

The 6-foot-7 right-hander threw 44 pitches at 100 mph or higher, reaching 104 mph on his initial offering to Freddie Freeman in the first. The Dodgers swung at 27 of his 62 fastballs, fouling off 16 and missing just five.

Misiorowski went 16-5 with a major league-low 1.80 ERA in 30 starts this season while averaging 100.6 mph with his four-seam fastball. He also led the majors with 252 strikeouts in 174 2/3 innings.

He struck out five and walked three in his second start this postseason. He tossed four innings of two-run ball in Milwaukee's 3-2 win over San Diego in Game 1 of their NL Division Series on Oct. 3, reaching triple digits on 52 of 88 pitches.

Misiorowski was helped by three inning-ending double plays against Los Angeles, including Kiké Hernández's bouncer to shortstop with the bases loaded in the second.

DL Hall replaced Misiorowski and got Freeman to ground into a double play, delighting the yellow towel-waving crowd of 42,617.

title: WATCH: Ravens finally find end zone with Henry receiving TD vs Falcons
description: The Baltimore Ravens finally got in the end zone on an 18-yard receiving touchdown by running back Derrick Henry. Atlanta is still on top 17-15.
fullText:
The Atlanta Falcons managed to keep Baltimore Ravens running back Derrick Henry out of the end zone for more than 40 minutes. However, he finally got into the end zone on an 18-yard reception for Baltimore's first touchdown of the game.

Here is a look at the touchdown, courtesy of the NFL's official social media:

Derrick Henry takes the screen pass to the end zone! 👑@BALvsATL on NBC/Peacock
Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/lcACs76ggy

It was Henry's first receiving touchdown since October of 2024 and his eighth touchdown this season. He now has a touchdown in every game this year. After his touchdown, the Ravens went for a two-point conversion to tie the game, but the conversion failed. So, Atlanta is still on top 17-15.

On their first drive of the second half, the Falcons had a 10-play drive that stalled in the red zone and they settled for a field goal. Both teams have struggled inside of the 20 yard line and have a combined four field goals, three for the Ravens and one for Atlanta.

Baltimore was able to force a fourth-down stop to get the ball back to their offense with a chance to take their first lead since their opening drive of the first quarter.

title: Lotus Improv on the NeXT
description: "Cult classic" isn't a term typically applied to software, but if it were, this would be its poster child.
fullText:
It is spoken of in reverent tones, invoked like a magic spell, whispered about as one of the mythical "roads not taken" in computing history. Its proponents write glowing reports and fawning YouTube reviews, lamenting its failure in the historical marketplace, each offering some justification for it not having set the world ablaze. It is safe to say, the legend of Lotus Improv persists to this day.

If we put ourselves in Steve Jobs's shoes circa 1988, it's easy to see why he would have been smitten by an early preview of what we now call a "pivot table." NeXT was struggling to find its market, and exclusives which justified a system purchase were sorely needed. "Maybe Improv can do for NeXT what VisiCalc did for the Apple II," must surely have crossed Jobs's mind. In making it a NeXT exclusive, Improv seemed to be a clear-eyed, forward-looking answer to the question dogging the company, posed by the inaugural issue of NeXTWORLD Magazine, "Why NeXT?"

Both NeXT and Improv brought innovative solutions to their respective computing questions of the day. NeXT made UNIX palatable to those scared of the terminal, debuted Display Postscript on a mega-pixel display, and made development for the system a snap. Improv rethought multi-dimensional data modeling, offered English-like formulas, and made it easy to rearrange data views on a whim.

The bones of both remain to this day. NeXT's operating system, NeXTSTEP / OPENSTEP, morphed into macOS, and by extension iOS. Lotus abandoned Improv fairly quickly, but a quick survey of today's spreadsheets shows a universal embrace of pivot tables.

Even today, it feels like nothing else, and still does data tricks no other spreadsheet can do as elegantly. Given its mythos, I feel a kind of nerd obligation to love it.

Events have converged to make this the right time to finally talk about Lotus Improv. First, it is time once again for "International Spreadsheet Day." Second, as Improv was initially a NeXT exclusive, it seems only appropriate to take a look at that machine here on the 15th (!) anniversary of the passing of Steve Jobs. Third, and not to toot my own horn too loudly, it is the 1st anniversary of this very blog.

Lotus Improv was one of four pieces of software I had in mind when deciding to start Stone Tools. In fact, it was quite literally the software that first triggered the thought, "I wish I had a place to talk about stuff like this." Deluxe Paint, the first post, was also one of those four. There are two yet to go; place your bets.

The trouble was, while I knew Deluxe Paint intimately and could jump right in, I simply had no real experience with other categories of productivity software. It would have been impossible to judge Improv fairly without first getting better acquainted with the landscape into which it was born. So, I bided my time.

Boy, howdy, do I want to impress upon you the superhuman restraint I've exhibited in waiting a full year to examine Improv.

I think we all understand Improv, being a spreadsheet, knows how to calculate sums and transcendentals and other mathematical goodness. "It does math!" is not a particularly compelling justification for its existence, nor to support its claim as the "NeXT generation of spreadsheets." Instead, let's get to know it by studying examples which show off its unique strengths, and with the suggestion of the book Improv 2.1 Revealed! we'll model up some good ole' American baseball, a game I love and understand completely.

Industry historians are far more capable of discussing the exile and homecoming of one Mr. Steven Paul Jobs back to Apple. I touched on the TL;DR of it in the timeline, and if you're really clamoring for juicy tidbits, a book was published this very year that delivers on that front.

While NeXT hardware was well regarded, it never really caught on. In the long run, the better result of NeXT engineering was NeXTSTEP and how neatly it wrapped UNIX in a clean, user-friendly, graphical interface. It's quite an accomplishment.

For me, it was the technology behind NeXTSTEP/OPENSTEP developer tools, Objective-C and Interface Builder, that kickstarted my programming career when those became the OS X development environment (hat tip to Aaron Hillegass's Cocoa Bootcamp at the Big Nerd Ranch). Even today, years after the advent of iOS and Swift, NeXT technology remains in the Foundation layer of Apple software, as denoted by NS-prefixed classes (a name-spacing trick from the Objective-C days).

For this investigation, I'm using NeXTSTEP 3.3, the last version before transitioning to OPENSTEP. NeXTSTEP looks and feels like a modern system, with some choice differences. Familiarity with any modern operating system, especially macOS, will inoculate you from breaking out into hives using it.

Considering the eye-candy Jobs seemed excited to add to OS X after the Apple merger, NeXTSTEP is positively staid; nothing here screams "lickable." If you've ever wondered what Susan Kare could have achieved if she'd had a larger canvas and palette (NeXTSTEP is 2-bit) than the original Mac, look no further. I like it.

The dock is present, though more rigid than the playful fluidity it acquired when transitioning to OS X. No "genie effects" nor dynamic magnification; it is ever-present and doesn't hide itself when not in use. Some applications change the dock icon when running (like Mail), while other applications do not (like Edit). One odd quirk is how the dock indicates running apps, by the absence of three dots on an icon tile. That's a strange choice, decorating the inactive icons.

File browsing adds a little complexity to system usage. The file browser contains its own mini-dock for favorites, the path to the currently selected item rendered as giant icons, and the file browser proper. Dragging files and folders around can only be done with an item's full-size icon. If you're browsing in list view, you can't drag list items into a folder or the dock, for example. Bit of a head-scratcher, that one.

Menuing for all applications is handled via a user-positionable, vertical menu. Sticking the menu somewhere sets its position for the active application, and every application can have its own position. You could theoretically have the menu jumping around all over the place as you hop between apps. Thankfully, it can also be called up at the current mouse position with a right-click; shades of RISC OS.

Also, good news for those who love the spinning beach ball on macOS! You'll feel that little ASMR tingle when it appears, especially if you run a color workstation. It's funny the things that can make something feel like "home."

Honestly, my biggest issue in adjusting to NeXTSTEP is the mouse. By default, it feels weird to use, with a dual-level acceleration curve, one for slow movement, one for fast. Crossing the threshold between "slow" and "fast" jumps the cursor across the screen when the alternate acceleration curve kicks in. I could never find my cursor except when moving the mouse verrrryyyy slooowwllllyyyy. Luckily, the emulator Previous has tools to help compensate (check "Sharpening the Stone").

Overall, you'll only need to adjust your thinking a little here and there, forget some modern habits, and you should be comfortable with NeXTSTEP in short order. 35 years later, it still looks and feels much like any modern operating system.

Almost depressingly so? Maybe that's a topic for another day.

Question: what is interesting about the following screenshot from Improv?

Answer: it contains all information necessary to build a copy for yourself. All data, formulas, dimensions, and relationships are exposed and visible. I note this not to suggest that screenshots are a great way to share Improv worksheets with others, though you could; the sheet above was rebuilt from a screenshot, in fact. Rather, I want to illustrate how "graspable" data can be in Improv's environment. Its formulas read naturally, and value references match the item names in the table. The work does what it claims.

Let's interrogate that a little more thoroughly.

To understand Improv is to forget what we know about spreadsheets. Slash commands? Never heard of him. B1? J93? K12 = int(A14 * lookup(B2..B7))? The ramblings of a madman. Rather than generic alphanumeric column/row identifiers, we define our rows and columns with "categories of items" specific to our domain.

Put another way, instead of asserting, "Columns A to L represent the months, and rows 1 through 31 represent the days," we will create a category called "months" and define twelve items for it named "January," "February," etc. and we will create a category called "days" and define 31 of those.

Take a look at these comparative videos which illustrate the difference. First, I'll use LibreOffice Calc to create a months/days grid, apply a value to January 1, and calculate December 31 as a multiple of January 1.

Here's how that same table is created in Improv. There are three things to note: how sequential items are generated, how categories are named (not strictly necessary for this simple example), and how formulas are created/applied.

There's a lot to absorb, I know, starting with how a new, blank worksheet consists of a single cell, not an infinite table of empty cells. Improv works with only and precisely the data we define. Where in the LibreOffice example we attached meaning to the columns by adding labels to the top of each column, that was for our benefit not Calc's.

I could, just to feel the warm, snuggly blanket of classic column/row naming, make an Improv category called "columns" and name my items A, B, C, etc. and a category called rows, with names 1, 2, 3, etc. Were we to take such a pedestrian approach to categories and items, we would diminish the magic of Improv's formula builder.

The bottom panel holds all formulas, which are applied at the granularity defined, in the order shown. In the example, I specified December:1 = but could just as easily have targeted all of December by specifying December = . That single formula would apply to every list item in December without needing to copy formulas through to each cell, nor set absolute/relative markers for cell references.

Here's a simple expansion of the previous table. Every day in January increases by 10%, and its corresponding day in December doubles the January value.

The two formulas shown are the only two formulas for the entire worksheet. I want to stress this; there are no other formulas lurking inside cells, hidden from view, waiting to be revealed by a selection or editing process. There are no duplicated formulas per cell, each increasing a relative cell reference by * 1.1 . We simply refer to categories (in this case "months" or "days"), items (as "January" or "27"), or specific intersections (as "April:19"), including relativity signifiers [THIS] , [PREV] , and [NEXT].

You might be thinking of ways to trick the system; to confuse and befuddle it. Why would you want to bully an old app like that? What did Improv do to deserve such shabby treatment? "What if two items have the same name? What if two formulas target the same cell?" Fret not, all shall be revealed and you will feel proper shame at trying to confuse this old program.

In the above example I have renamed one of the Days as "March," to create ambiguity when referencing "March." Does "March" mean the Day or the Month now? We can be explicit, referring to Months:March. Note though that if we aren't explicit, Improv will be on to our tricks and call us out, as in formula 5.

In formula 2, I set December:15 to the static value 1000. In formula 3, I also set it to be calculated as "double its corresponding January value." Note the "overlap" icon (two intersecting squares) on those formulas and the Overlap text in the cell. Clicking the overlap icon gives us an opportunity to resolve ambiguity by explicitly selecting which formula should win for that cell.

Cleanly handling formula ambiguity was originally seen by the prototype team as an intractable engineering problem. From "Improv: The Inside Story", by Simson L. Garfinkel, NeXTWORLD, Fall 1991:

Personally, I like Improv's solution. I honestly think more software should be very dumb, and not try to intuit or guess what I want. Tell me the problem in clear language, and provide the simplest tool that gives me the most control over problem resolution. Be smart about helping me, don't try to help me by being smart.

Before we get in too deep, I want to make sure I note Improv's beautiful help system, replete with index and search. Considering the difficulty in tracking down a manual for the NeXT release, having this available during my exploration proved invaluable. It's neatly illustrated, with terse (sometimes overly terse) descriptions of the tools, hyperlinked to other pages of the documentation, as warranted. Improv felt it could do even better than that and made its help contextual.

The Help system, when invoked, defaults to displaying documentation for whatever is currently selected in the user interface. That's very useful, but becomes supercharged with "Point for Help," as demonstrated in the video above. This turns the cursor into a ? symbol, and whatever we click will be revealed in the Help window.

This is a great idea, because I don't always know what Lotus wants to call some little interface doohickey, so I don't know what to search for. Now I know: the "Calc" button is a "Status Indicator" and the triangle icon that sometimes shows up is the "Formula Error Indicator." Pork chop sandwiches.

Looking through Usenet archives, I saw this called "toilet paper" by at least one person. Lotus called it the "item dispenser." It's an interesting first attempt to do something we take for granted today and only exists in the NeXT version of Improv. It's cute, but smacks of someone being overly excited with new development toys.

If we need to generate a list of items to populate an axis of your data, this tool generates sequential list items for you. It does its best to kind of "guess" our intentions, so if we type in "Sunday," then pull down on the dispenser, days of the week will be auto-generated in a list. We then "tear off" the list, which loads the cursor with the items, which we attach to an existing item, appending that category with the loaded list items.

That means we need to have at least one item in a category onto which the list can be attached. This is annoying, because the existing item likely has no relationship to the generated list. I'm always having to make a list, attach it to an existing item, then delete the original, unrelated item. These days, we can type directly into a cell and extend that cell intelligently across adjacent cells. In fact, Lotus would switch to that methodology when migrating Improv over to Windows for version 2. Hold ALT and drag an existing item to get the same effect.

The original dispenser truly is a feature that could only have been thought up within the NeXT environment. I don't hold it against the devs for getting excited by the GUI flexibility Interface Builder afforded. I, too, did the same back in the early OS X 10.2 days. It practically begged us to play around with GUI ideas, remixing elements into new configurations. "First Responder" and "bindings" stans, represent!

One of the great features of that development environment was how easy it was to “say ‘No’ a thousand times” while trying ideas. Lotus embraced that, achieving quickly on NeXT what had blocked their progress on OS/2 and Microsoft's Presentation Manager.

The "item dispenser" was singled out as a specific tool that benefitted from Interface Builder; there really wasn't anything similar to its rapid, iterative, GUI development at the time. In fact, I might go so far as to say there's nothing quite like it today, even from Apple.

Joel Spolsky, in editing The Best Software Writing I, added a personal aside on Lotus Improv, blaming its failure thusly, "Improv required you to define strict n-dimensional hypercubes for your data. There was none of the flexibility of traditional spreadsheets."

I suppose if one wanted to paint Improv in the most inhospitable light, Spolsky is correct. In practice, it doesn't feel as impenetrable as his description. However, I do think he's on to something that gets at the heart of why Improv never gained traction.

For now, let's hold our collective nose and dive into the scary, foreboding waters of "n-dimensional hypercubes" and model up some baseball. Our first dimension will be Year.

Let's add a League dimension next.

Next, we'll get more granular and add Division. Internally, Improv separates our work into three parts: data, views, and formulas. What we see on screen is just Improv's best-effort to represent our three-dimensional data flattened out into a two-dimensional view. Improv adds extra columns to the view, as necessary, to ensure we always see the full extent of our data relationships.

Now, we'll add some win/loss data and the next thing you know we’ve built a 4-dimensional hypercube. Are we scared yet?

Since I've only modeled at the "Division" level, I'll add together divisional wins inline to calculate the totals and... hmmm... "No dice," as they say in baseball (Presumably. Are dice involved in baseball?)

Alas and alack, we can only enter concrete numbers, dates, or text into cells; any formula, no matter how trivial, must go into the Formula Panel (bottom). In this case, I could add a formula that targets a specific cell, as American:East:2020:Win = 40 + 33 + 32 + 25 + 24, but the whole point of a spreadsheet is to automate that kind of junk for me. I suppose the path of least resistance is to add a Teams category to add up all team wins and, wait a second...

Dang it, that petard I confidently told myself wouldn't hoist me has come around to do precisely that. Here we see the downside of dimensional modeling, at least for the layperson, and arguably for most typical spreadsheet users. It all looks like a neat little chart, but that word "dimension" describes and reveals the problem. To add a category, its items necessarily apply to all other categories. Teams don't do that; they are unique to each League and Division.

But we just might have a way out.

Lotus engineers clearly understood that categories alone weren't going to cut it. Categories impose rigidity to our data that does not always accommodate the messiness of real data. We need another way to organize our data.

Groups are intra-category, named collections of sequential items. Make a category and add a bunch of individual items. Select a sequential group of some subset of items and group them, giving that group a unique name. Once everything is grouped, groups of groups can be grouped to group a group of ... wait, I got myself confused. Groups can be grouped, 'nuff said.

With "Teams," we quickly run into a side-effect of groups, and how it can necessitate a cascade effect across multiple categories. I want to add teams and group them by "Division," but that forces me to also make "League" a group as well. What was three categories have now collapsed into one: "Teams"

Here's what that looks like in practice.

We still gain the benefit of name references in formulas, as in the above untethered-to-reality example. A reference to East would apply to both American and National, unless we specify by . as in National.East and American.East

Groups can be subtotaled, using the groupsum() function, as you can see in this more data-rich chart of the MLB stats from 2022 to 2026. Notice, however, we risk a conflict for Percent in our Total field, where there are two formulas battling it out for dominance over the same cell calculation. The handy SKIP keyword will skip (i.e. "won't apply this formula to") groups, cells, items, and categories as designated.

Groups helped bring granularity and specificity to our data structure, but the more categories we remove, the more we remove access to the very feature that has kept Improv in the back of nerd minds for decades. You know what I'm talking about.

FINALLY we get to the point those in the know have been anxious to talk about, "Lotus Improv invented pivot tables. It says so right there in Wikipedia."

At this stage of my knowledge of all things retro productivity, I think the most I'm willing to concede right now is that Lotus Improv likely invented pivot tables as we understand them today. But, like Yoda coyly teasing the existence of Luke's sister to a guy who should have already known about her, there is another program, a future Stone Tools subject, that may lay claim to the title of "first pivot table." I exercise my right, as "guy who runs the blog," to reserve final judgement on this point until then.

For our purposes today, it's a true enough statement and the inventor even has a nice video on YouTube in which he shows it off to Lotus staff for the first time. Meet Pito Salas, inventor of the pivot table.

Salas, now retired, developed the idea while working for Lotus Development's Advanced Technology Group. He put together a fakey version of his vision, a kind of slideshow, showing off the things he wanted to be able to do: English-like formulas, multi-dimensional data, and rearrangeable views into the data. He was given the greenlight to proceed, "All those [ideas] I had described with hand waving,'' recalls Pito. "I had no clue how to build it." A year of nose-to-the-grindstone later, and a prototype dubbed "Back Bay" went on US tour, wowing financial modelers. Everyone who saw it, wanted it.

Let's take a look at how Improv handles pivoting. To start, I'm leaving it empty of data, so we can focus on the dynamic view structure more easily. Then, I'll move categories around to show how the view flexes to present the data. Next, I'll put categories into the third axis, called a "Page Category," allowing us to paginate our data. Finally, I'll enter a formula and a little data to show off a trick pivot table contemporaries cannot perform.

Now I'm going to try and replicate this in LibreOffice Calc v26.8. There are a few things to note, but let's first point and laugh at the fumbling attempts of a LibreOffice newbie (me).

A few things jumped out at me while comparing these approaches. First, modeling up a relatively complex data set in Improv is as easy as thinking about it, and the presentation of the data matches my mental model. LibreOffice requires me to bridge a fairly wide conceptual gap between what I want and how I model it, due to the amount of redundant data I have to enter for every line item.

Some items, like "League," translate cleanly, while "Record" does not. In fact, I'm still unclear what the best approach would be to convert my Improv computed item "Win Ratio." LibreOffice has the concept of a "computed field" inside pivot tables, but reaching across columns to pluck out related data to perform computations is complicated.

In Apple Numbers, Microsoft Excel, Google Sheets, and LibreOffice, pivot table data is splintered off into a separate snapshot of the data, dedicated to the pivot table view. Pivot table data can typically be lightly manipulated, but does not affect the original data. The reverse can be done, but only after asking for an explicit update of the pivot table to reflect changes to the primary data table. This is a huge drop-off in ease-of-use from the Improv way of things where every view of the data directly manipulates the base data.

Dragging around categories is just as easy in either approach, though Improv gives immediate drag-and-drop access to what LibreOffice calls a "Filter," i.e. a paged view, and generally "feel better," IMHO. LibreOffice requires us to open up a separate panel and drag things around in there. I will say, however, that being able to filter the filters (i.e. exclude/include specific subsets of data) is handy.

Sheets, Numbers, and Excel (online version) are all strictly panel-based pivoting. Interestingly enough, the panel approach is precisely the interface Lotus rejected, at the behest of Steve Jobs. Once more, from the Garfinkel article.

Having now directly compared Improv's approach to dynamic views against modern pivot tables, it is safe to say they are the same only so much as wagyu beef with gruyere cheese prepared by Gordon Ramsay and the sawdust at the bottom of a Happy Meal are both "cheeseburgers." Improv tastes much better.

A Lotus invention which debuted in Lotus 1-2-3, "named ranges" have attempted to bring order to the chaos of cell identifiers. In 1-2-3, Range > Name > Create will apply a name of choice to a defined cell range, after which that range can be referenced in formulas by that name. So, in 1-2-3 or any modern spreadsheet we can name range F1..F23 as Sales and sum(Sales) will work.

Superficially, this looks similar to how Improv works with categories and items for multi-dimensional data. However, named ranges are for convenience only, and do not establish relationships between data values. In Improv, Sales would represent a fundamental aspect of a piece of data. Getting the sum of all sales is the same, sum(Sales), but it being a dimension on the data gives us deeper options. For a specific year, sum(2020:Sales) will match against two axes at once. sum(2020:Arkansas:Sales) could further pinpoint our summation.

Let's see how this would be done with modern spreadsheets and named ranges. If we want to mimic Improv's dimensional relationships, we must define relationships of interest within each formula, (and those formulas have to be copied over to every related cell) such that:

Of course we could substitute hardcoded filter criteria with values pulled from a lookup, or perhaps extract equated values via a LET statement. Maybe even set up a little sub-table to hold calculated values. Quickly this gets way more complicated than I'd have hoped for, so personally I'd resort to doing it the old-fashioned way and just hardcode in a bunch of cell references. To reiterate, the complete solution for an entire sheet in Improv, where win/loss information is its own dimension, is the single formula:

The last of the big features, which takes advantage of NeXT's graphics prowess, is the charting functionality. Creating a chart launches an entirely separate application, Presentation Builder, which has grand plans on becoming PageMaker when it grows up.

Generating a chart generates a full, blank page onto which a chart is placed. A suite of palettes complements the charting workflow, allowing for precision edits of the chart, its titles, colors, positioning, and more within the full page. Multiple charts can be generated and placed on the same page. Arbitrary text and shapes, lines pointing at interesting bits, and even sound annotations (a system-wide NeXT tool, called "Lip Service") can be placed at will.

So it goes that while we have the tools to place arbitrary text on the page, yet lack tools to center that text, the sense that Lotus has overextended itself is strong. Sometimes it's enough to just generate the output a program excels at, and leave "page composition" to the professionals. Again, I need software to be more dumb. That's without even mentioning the plethora of formatting tools scattered amongst an unreasonable number of palettes, panels, and "inspectors."

A benefit of these tools on the NeXT is that everything we do is Postscript by default, thanks to NeXT's Display Postscript screen rendering engine. "Print" a document as PostScript, and we can render the resultant .ps file on any modern system. I opened it directly in Affinity and received precisely what I saw in Improv, chopped off text and all, but like, high-quality chopped off text.

Look, I try my best to craft a compelling narrative, moving from topic to topic, stitching together callbacks and observations to lead you, my dear reader, on a carefully considered ride. It's just you and me, side by side at the keyboard, chatting about software and learning together. But, sometimes there's junk I need to squeeze in that I can't find a natural segue for discussing. Here, then, is a brain dump of other things I want you to know about Improv.

In 1993, NeXT abandoned its hardware initiative and moved over to Intel, rebranding as NeXT Software, releasing OPENSTEP soon after. At the same time, Improv also moved over to Intel, but parted ways with NeXT. With version 2, Lotus developers achieved the success that eluded them on OS/2, porting Improv over to Windows 3.1.

The feature set for version 2 is disappointingly similar to version 1, and by this time competing software was starting to embrace some of Improv's unique qualities. We do finally get undo, so thank Kapor for small favors. Scripting arrives in the form of LotusScript. A new Windows UI adds a bunch of buttons to the interface, and flushes the toilet paper dispenser for a more sensible list generator.

That's basically it for the new stuff, but at least they kept the old problems as well.

Cell reference relativity is still locked to a single dimension. Formulas cannot be freely rearranged, only cut-and-pasted into position. No 3D worksheets. Then, to throw a little extra wrinkle into the mix, there was Lotus's product strategy on the PC. If Improv wasn't your thing, maybe their other Windows spreadsheet, 1-2-3/Windows, would feel more comfortable. Or their other-other option, Lotus Symphony. Or their other-other-other option, Lotus Works. Or their other-other-other-other option, Lotus 1-2-3 for DOS Release 4, which went on sale in 1994.

Regardless, it was well-liked by the press, even if reviewers didn't seem comfortable giving full-throated endorsements. Take this Compute, July 1994, review for example.

Or this PC World, February 1994, review.

It would be hard to intuit, based on that review, that PC World had declared Improv the "Winner" in the Applications category for their 10th Annual Awards for Technical Excellence just a few months prior.

3 in spirit, if not in flesh; let's take a quick look at Quantrix, the product I clumsily foreshadowed earlier.

From ex-Lighthouse CEO (also ex-Sun CEO) Jonathan Schwartz's blog, "In 1989, a few friends and I started a software company, Lighthouse Design, that devoted itself to the NeXT platform. Whether any of us admitted it at the time, Lighthouse was built by a group of people for whom Steve Jobs was the gravitational center of the universe."

Their devotion to Jobs was returned in favor, by way of advice for their products to flourish on NeXT. Ultimately, according to Schwartz, the problem was less about finding a way for Lighthouse to flourish on NeXT than it was about getting NeXT to flourish in the first place. When looking for a buyout in Lighthouse's waning days, they had fingers crossed to be acquired by NeXT but Jobs didn't bite. They were bought by Sun, their products shoved in a vault never to see the light of day.

With Microsoft unwilling to support the platform, Lighthouse made the closest thing to an Office suite for NeXT. They built programming tools, project management software, a presentation tool called Concurrence (that Jobs used and which "inspired" Keynote), and two spreadsheet programs: ParaSheet and Quantrix.

ParaSheet took the more traditional approach, while Quantrix was just a flat-out clone of Improv, I don't know how else to say it. It has the same split screen worksheet/formulas, the same THIS NEXT PREV formula tools, the same draggable categories, it imports Improv documents, and more. According to one Hacker News reader, "The manuals were interchangeable."

Lighthouse took the ideas behind Improv and ran with them, envisioning what a possible v3 could have been. Put simply, everything I've expressed frustration with in Improv is addressed in Quantrix.

It has undo. It has drag-and-drop, reorderable formulas. It has scripting. It has cross-worksheet category synchronization. The "Item Dispenser" is replaced with an in-line widget; pull to expand like any modern spreadsheet does today. It has multi-dimensional cell relativity. It runs on OPENSTEP for Intel, as well as NeXTSTEP on Motorola 68K . It has color. It loses contextual help (can't win 'em all). And that morass of panels and palettes for editing the charts I showed earlier? Those are collapsed into a single, tidy "Inspector."

Long story short? If you want to experience the best version of Lotus Improv today, use Lighthouse Quantrix v2.3. You'll get all of the original, cool tools built better, with a more sensible interface. Plus, Lighthouse gave away their NeXT applications, with license code, for free. How neat is that?

The big twist, for those affording me a generous definition of "twist," is that Quantrix still exists. It is alive and being sold for "ask for quote," so I think I'll just put this credit card back in my wallet at this time. Today, it very explicitly targets the professional, high-end, financial modeling crowd, and not the general-purpose masses. You know, the crowd that Lotus first showed their Back Bay prototypes to back in the day (see timeline). Its self-introductory video pivots (get it?) many of its 35-year-old features as revolutionary. A back-handed indictment of the stagnation of an industry, or a product finally finding its niche? You be the judge!

It's hard to suss out precisely what happened, but I found a little information floating around the Quantrix forums. If that is to be trusted, Lighthouse's Quantrix chief engineer, Pete Murray, founded the company Subx and rebuilt Quantrix as a Java application in 2003. Quantrix's website says it was acquired by IDBS in 2010. I'm still completely in the dark how Quantrix escaped Sun's containment field, as Sun had refused to sell off the Lighthouse apps to hungry buyers; that stuff could have been converted into OS X apps in the early days.

At any rate, it is one of the more handsome JRE applications, while suffering from telltale Java rendering issues, especially with regard to text positioning and scaling. Otherwise it is clean and inoffensive. Sterile? Boring. That's the word I was looking for: boring. "It knows its target audience," is perhaps more charitable.

So where does this leave my relationship with Lotus Improv? Why did I dangle that "And yet..." at the start of the post? If I'm completely honest with myself, there is a vibrating tension between "wanting to love it" and "actually loving it."

After all of these weeks, I think I'm in a pretty good position to suggest why it didn't take the world by storm: it's not a great spreadsheet program. Let me qualify that statement lest r/Improv4Life roasts me alive; the roasting can wait a moment.

For what it does, it is amazing and even fun to use. What it doesn't do is provide a good, general purpose spreadsheet experience to the masses. It claimed to do that, positioning itself as the "NeXT generation of spreadsheets." Whatever Lotus Improv did or did not accomplish for the spreadsheet genre, one thing is for certain: it makes a fantastic tech demo.

Seen in that light, I'd have been as sold on it as Jobs was, excitedly showing it to NeXT non-believers, "Look what MY computer can do!" Those moments of smug technological superiority amongst friends are fun, aren't they? Once you played with it for a week or two, and the initial excitement of pivoting dulled, you may have ashamedly harbored a bit of buyer's remorse.

Adam Bosworth, in an article contemplating a talk he gave at ICSOC '04, was thinking about software complexity vs. simplicity, and posited:

Paradoxically, Improv's promise to improve data comprehensibility wound up narrowing its general appeal. Want to quickly throw down a few lines of data, like a makeshift phone directory? You're gonna have to rethink your data as a matrix of abstract qualities about your friends. Despite its friendly English-like formulas and delightful GUI for pivoting data, Improv is in actuality purpose-built for far more rigorous data modeling than its playful tools suggest.

It's the next generation of spreadsheets for a thin slice of the market.

That said, there is a non-zero set of readers for whom their hardcore number crunching needs perfectly align with Improv's promises. If that's you, you're absolutely going to fall in love...

Ways to improve the experience, notable deficiencies, workarounds, and notes about incorporating the software into modern workflows (if possible).

Improv does export to Lotus 1-2-3, but you'll likely be disappointed with the results. Consider a table with formulas and calculated values in the cells. Everything you see in the cells will be exported, but there will be no formulas or relationships between anything. You will receive a snapshot of all current values, arranged to visually match the table structure you had when exporting. Improv's approach to shared formulas and multi-dimensional data simply don't have an elegant export solution to traditional spreadsheets.

If you have Improv documents you want to import into Quantrix, two criteria must be met. Save your Improv project as an .imx file (not the default .imp), and make sure you have the Lighthouse FilterServicer.service (available at the same site offering the Quantrix software link I mentioned under "Version 3") installed at ~/Library/Services.

Exporting charts is simplicity, thanks to Display Postscript. The Postscript files NeXTSTEP generates open and render just fine on modern machines, using Ghostscript or other graphics programs.

As mentioned previously, I actually recommend using Lighthouse Quantrix v2.3 instead of Lotus Improv, on the NeXT. The substantial features Improv lacks are numerous:

In general, it's lacking the clay-like malleability of a traditional spreadsheet. If you're doing what a lot of us do, using spreadsheets like a kind of mini-database, you'll probably get frustrated.

title: Did Cooper Kupp have a first down? Why Seahawks WR was ruled short in game-ending decision
description: Seahawks fans were furious after Cooper Kupp was ruled short of a first down against the 49ers, effectively ending the game.
fullText:
Did Cooper Kupp have a first down? Why Seahawks WR was ruled short in game-ending decision originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

The Seahawks were a total mismatch for the 49ers in the playoffs last season, but there was little separation between the two NFC West rivals on Sunday. In fact, the game came down to as little as an inch.

Looking to keep Seattle's drive alive in the final minute of the fourth quarter, Sam Darnold found Cooper Kupp for just about 10 yards on a fourth-and-10, but Kupp's outstretched hands as he went out of bounds were controversially ruled short of the marker.

While the Seahawks' raucous crowd cheered as they saw the replay, the officials came back with a different ruling than the fans were expecting.

Darnold threw short of the line to gain on fourth-and-10, but Kupp was able to break free from a defender and take aim at the first-down marker. As he tried to evade Malik Mustapha, Kupp leapt forward with the ball and landed along the sideline.

Cooper Kupp is short and the @49ers take over! @SFvsSEA on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus https://t.co/k9426I2gFe

Officials ruled Kupp short on the field. Replay showed the it was about as bang-bang as it gets. Kupp never stepped out of bounds and clearly got the ball past the marker at some point, but the question officials had to answer was whether the ball was over the while out-of-bounds line before it reached the first-down marker.

Cooper Kupp was ruled short of a 1st down on this 4th and 10. Seahawks turnover on downs https://t.co/BZTFctlLvz

It's extraordinarily difficult to tell whether the ball is over the white line and out of bounds when it's at least a couple of feet above the line, so officials didn't have convincing evidence to overturn the call on the field.

In the pool report, officials said there was "nothing clear and obvious" to overturn the call on the field.

The call stood, rather than being confirmed, which indicates Kupp would have been given the first down had the call on the field been a first down.

Instead, the Seahawks turned the ball over on downs and suffered a 32-29 home loss that could seriously damage their NFC West chances.

title: Why Dre Greenlaw was ejected from Seahawks-49ers after confrontation with helmet-less Ernest Jones
description: The linebacker crossed the line with a few decisions.
fullText:
Why Dre Greenlaw was ejected from Seahawks-49ers after confrontation with helmet-less Ernest Jones originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

In a battle of two of the best teams in the NFL, Dre Greenlaw may have changed the game with an early exit.

In the first half of the game between the Seattle Seahawks vs. the San Francisco 49ers, Greenlaw made a few decisions that led to an ejection. First, he committed a penalty on Sam Darnold, then he got into a confrontation with Ernest Jones that crossed the line.

Greenlaw is an NFL veteran who knows how important these divisional games are, making this mistake even more crucial. The 49ers will now have to try to win the road game without one of their starting linebackers on the field.

This is why Greenlaw got an early ejection on Sunday afternoon.

MORE: Full details of Marvin Harrison Jr. trade to Texans

On a play in the second quarter, Greenlaw was initially penalized for a late hit on Seahawks quarterback Sam Darnold, handing Seattle an extra 15 yards. However, it was Greenlaw's actions after the fact that that got him ejected from the game.

As the Seahawks bench approached Greenlaw to defend their quarterback, Greenlaw headbutted Seattle linebacker Ernest Jones, who was without a helmet on the sidelines. The officials decided that the headbutt was worthy of an ejection.

I have no problem with what Dre Greenlaw did to Sam Darnold. It’s a bang bang play and Dre has to force him out of bounds My issue is the extra bs after the play by Dre And he’s kicked out of the game because of it https://t.co/cRP3Ne1LrE

Dre Greenlaw ejected after headbutting Jones on the sideline https://t.co/hCXUxZm4sg

The NFL instituted a new rule this year that allows referees to eject players on plays that don't draw penalty flags. In this case, the league apparently told the refs to eject Greenlaw.

49ers LB Dre Greenlaw was ejected for headbutting Seahawks LB Ernest Jones IV under a new rule that allows the league office to eject players for non-football acts even if they're not flagged. The NFL saw the replay and told officials to disqualify him. https://t.co/QpxUhe9kl2

The officials gave a more detailed explanation of the ejection in the postgame pool report.

"The clubs passed a rule this year that the [Art McNally Gameday Central] can actually eject a player even when there is not a flag down on the field for the action," Vice President of Instant Replay Mark Butterworth said. "We have a very specific process we go through. Troy Vincent let us know that the player was ejected, so then I communicated with the field to inform them that number 57 was ejected from the game for a non-football act.

Greenlaw has been part of many heated 49ers-Seahawks games, so it's not a surprise that he was playing with an edge in this game. Still, the linebacker wasn't making the smart decision when he interacted with Jones on the sidelines.

After the game, Kyle Shanahan said he didn't see what happened but acknowledged that Greenlaw has to be better to stay in the game.

"We gotta be a lot smarter than that, can't do that," he said.

title: What we learned from Dallas' humiliating Week 5 loss to the Buccaneers
description: Dallas' defensive struggles against the run and the pass, plus turnovers, can allow any team a shot at upsetting the Cowboys
fullText:
The Dallas Cowboys have to forget the idea of "it's just the (insert bad team here)." The winless Tampa Bay Buccaneers, with a rookie undrafted free agent (UDFA) at quarterback, beat them on their own field, sending them to 2-3 on the season. Unlike most Dallas losses, this game wasn't just about an awful defense and poor special teams. The offense was bad as well, with two turnovers, a nonexistent rushing attack, and poor passing against the blitz.

The defense is the biggest issue, and they were against Tampa Bay. They allowed over six yards per attempt, giving up 241 rushing yards. The special teams committed a fumble on a kick return that put the Buccaneers up by two touchdowns, and the offense needed a 99-yard drive in the fourth quarter to reach 16 points. Everything about this loss was that one team was better in every area of the game, and that can be laid at the coaches' feet.

Scouting an opposing defense seems unnecessary when facing the Cowboys' defense. They allow mediocre offenses to get it together against them. Jaxson Dart had a quarterback rating of 134.2. Jayden Daniels and Marcus Mariota combined for a rating of 104.1. Lamar Jackson ended with a 136.7, and C.J. Stroud had a 126.7. Those are known quantities at QB, but Dallas was facing UDFA rookie Jaylon Daniels, not Baker Mayfield. It didn't matter in the end. Daniels threw 25 times, completing 19 for 189 yards and a touchdown, with a quarterback rating of 110.2. When any quarterback can start and feel comfortable moving the ball, every game becomes a four-quarter battle. Giving up 8 yards per rush to Bucky Irving is bad enough, but getting crushed in both areas is nearly impossible to handle, especially for a rookie play-caller at defensive coordinator.

The Cowboys took the opening drive of the game 70 yards on nine plays for a touchdown to get off to an excellent start, but the Dallas defense killed all momentum the next drive. Tampa Bay went on a 15-play, 73-yard drive that took 11 minutes off the clock and faced no more than a third-and-five. That is the type of drive the Buccaneers were looking for as a defensive strategy. Keep Dallas' offense off the field with long scoring drives. One first-quarter drive was all the Cowboys' offense got. Tampa Bay ran the ball 39 times, got 24 first downs, and held the ball nearly 40 minutes. They also converted a third-and-21 and a third-and-13 to extend drives.

The defense held Tampa Bay a few times, but when they finally gave up a big play and a quick score to start the second half, a tipped interception set up Tampa Bay inside the 30 and ended a Dallas scoring drive. The Buccaneers went on another touchdown drive to take a 21-10 lead. Then, a fumble on the kickoff return piled even more on. Tampa Bay added a field goal to go up two touchdowns. After a 99-yard Dallas touchdown drive and a failed two-point conversion, the Cowboys got the ball back down eight with a chance to tie, but the game ended on a Jake Ferguson drop that popped up and was intercepted by Alex Anzalone as the Cowboys drove for the tying touchdown. Multiple ways to play the blame game when a team plays so poorly, but the three turnovers were definitely key.

title: Writing a Game in C
description: The long version: what writing For the Common Wealth in plain C actually looks like
fullText:
I wrote a short post a while back about why I chose C. This is the longer one, about what it’s actually like building a game this size in it.

For the Common Wealth is about 175,000 lines of C, there are 658 source files. There’s no engine as such. There’s little separation between “engine code” and “game code”, which was… a choice. In my defence, what exists as an “engine” would work for unrelated 2.5D games, but it’s not a reusable engine for any random game, at all.

SDL3, plus SDL3_image to load the PNGs and SDL3_mixer for sound. That’s the lot. The Steam integration is loaded at runtime if Steam is there, so the same exe runs with or without it. The whole game is plain old C99.

I wanted to keep dependencies down to an absolute minimum, mostly because I saw myself releasing this game on retro platforms like Amiga, but that is looking doubtful unless SDL3 is fully GPU accelerated on an Amiga, and memory usage now means it would be PowerPC Amigas only.

Most of what appears during play lives in fixed-size pools that are set up once: sprites, explosions, particles, bullets, fires. A level asks for what it needs from those pools, and the pools are reset when the level restarts.

Levels, and the level builder (BIABuilder)

All 25 levels are built in BIABuilder, my level editor, which is C# and Avalonia rather than C. The file format is JSON, and on export BIABuilder writes each level out as plain binary, field after field, and the game reads it back in exactly the same order into its C structs. There’s no parser and no schema, just magic numbers at the end of records so I quickly know if I’ve got the export wrong.

BIABuilder is about 25,000 lines of C#.

Below is the same level in-game.

This is a 2.5D game… and that’s a stretch. Let’s call it a 2.1D game. It’s 2D through and through, but multiple sprite layers and isometric art make it look 3D. Ish. Some of the time.

Sprites are based on PNG images. There is no tiling system, you can put images anywhere you like, using BIABuilder. This can then be edited with transforms, hooks and events in BIABuilder and in-game, each sprite becomes a struct with 138 members.

The main sprite layer is called “Ordering” and orders sprites by the Y baseline every frame to allow player sprites to move in front of, and behind other sprites.

C has no reflection, so the level builder can’t just call a function by name. Instead, each level registers the functions it wants to expose under their own names, using a macro that turns a function’s name into a string. When BIABuilder says “when the player walks in here, call npc_escaped”, the game looks that name up when the level loads and keeps the function pointer. Most of the level-specific behaviour in the game, like a door opening or a car driving off, is one of these. These hooks are the main way in which behaviours and functions can get assigned in BIABuilder and run in-game. An example would be “player proximity” hook. Where any sprite can have this hook assigned, and the hook will be called in-game when the player approaches the sprite. This is ideal for opening doors and things like that.

NPCs run their “AI” in a thread pool. They patrol around location waypoints, but on becoming alerted or suspicious, they can break away from patrol and then start finding their own paths on an A* pathfinding system. They can attack, panic, run away, and talk amongst themselves.

There are several types of collision, Physical, can’t walk there, like a wall or a hole. Bullet, stops a bullet. Player Vision can computer controlled allies see there. NPC Vision, can NPCs see there. There is Patrol Collision which helps guide NPCs through sensible patrol routes, i.e. they can walk through a swamp if they want, but they’re not going to patrol that swamp. Finally, there is Hint Only collision, which is for things like tents. You can shoot straight through a tent, it won’t stop a bullet, but we do want sound effects of a bullet hitting cloth.

Weird name from back when this game was going to be a cozy RPG and a named area would be something like “Mr. Cozymans’s Orchard” or something. Now they are arbitrary polygons to which we apply effects like moving water, or clouds, or interact with other feature like rain. When there is a level with rain, we can make Named Areas for Rain Rejection so while rain can fall anywhere on the level, it can be stopped from falling in certain places, like indoors, or the side of a wall or something. The same applies to falling snow.

On starting a level, the BIABuilder exports are loaded from disk and a level is composed from sprites, named area, NPCs, locations, collision, mission objective, audio regions and hooks. Hooks are resolved from string at this point and during gameplay they are function pointers. NPCs start to think in their own thread pool, animations resolve into timelines which are simple structs which can advance an animation or transform based on the current ticks.

Timelines handle movement of just about everything in game, from walking to a bullet in flight. A bullet in flight is a discrete sprite that checks its own position every frame. It may hit collision, or a player, or an NPC, then the next event begins, like NPC death.

All characters in For the Common Wealth can emit “mutterings” which may be a scream on death, or it may be two NPCs talking with each other about their girlfriends back home. As well as enemy NPCs, there are “hostages” and “civilians”, with their own voices and motives.

C and SDL3 has suited me very well for making this game. I’ve made innumerable mistakes in making it, but none of them were caused by C. My mistakes came from never having made a game before, and learning as I went. C on the other hand has been great, and SDL has been rock solid throughout.

title: Can Decision Models (Like Jev) Plan Ahead?
description:
Introducion
Can decision models like Jev plan ahead? If so, how can we quantify their planning ability? …
fullText:
Can decision models like Jev plan ahead? If so, how can we quantify their planning ability?

This is the question that BeelineBench seeks to answer. In this article, I'll explain my methodology and share a few interesting results from the benchmark.

The core idea is simple. We present a decision model with a problem domain (like Blocks world) and a list of available actions, and ask it to select the next action in order to solve the problem. We repeat until the decision model has reached a solution, or has reached an evaluation cap. If the decision model explores few unnecessary moves before reaching a solution, the intuition is that the decision model is exhibiting an ability to plan ahead while selecting an action.

To compute the beeline metric, we first count the number of nodes along a shortest path found using a breadth-first search. We then divide by the number of nodes explored by the decision model while finding a solution.

A perfect score is 1, meaning that the decision model reached a solution by exploring exactly the minimum number of nodes.

We include baselines against random-choice and a classic heuristic as deciders. N=100 trials are drawn for each problem domain, and 95% confidence intervals are bootstrapped from the scores. We also compute a number of ancillary metrics and diagnostics.

In four of seven problem domains, at least one decider model was able to beat the heuristic-based baseline. All included decider models beat random choice on all problems. Rush Hour was by far the most difficult problem for decider models. The decider models seemed to handle Wikispeedia and "Keys and Doors" quite well.

A few models appear frequently on the frontier, including Mercury Decide and pplx-decider 1.0.

We plan on including additional models and curating our problem domains. Expense is a factor, so we appreciate donations through Github.

BeelineBench is a portable, configurable, reproducible, and re-randomizable benchmark. Each problem domain consists of 100 trials. The trials are randomly drawn from each domain, with an optional master seed for re-randomization. 95% confidence intervals are bootstrapped from each model's result for each problem domain.

The bench is designed to plug in new models, new problems, and to gracefully handle restarts. A PyPi package and Docker containers are included.

title: Gh-pull – A local GitHub PR dashboard using your existing CLI login
description: Fast local GitHub pull request dashboard with grouping, review status, and PR editing - shiqicao/gh-pull
fullText:
much better github pr dashboard

A fast, local GitHub pull request dashboard. Group PRs by repository, search with GitHub qualifiers, track reviews and checks, and manage your own PRs from one view.

Both use your existing GitHub CLI login or a personal access token. No separate GitHub App installation is required. You can access the repositories your credentials allow, subject to your organization's token and SSO policies. A GitHub.com account is required; GitHub Enterprise hosts are not supported.

Install GitHub CLI if needed, then run:

gh pull starts the dashboard in the background and opens your browser. Running it again reopens the same instance. No clone, Node installation, or GitHub App installation is needed. Closing the browser leaves the dashboard running until you stop it or shut down your computer; it does not register a system startup service.

The extension listens only on 127.0.0.1. It prefers port 3000 and chooses a free port if needed. An explicit --port fails if occupied. It inherits GH_TOKEN / GITHUB_TOKEN when supplied; otherwise it uses gh auth token --hostname github.com.

Update with gh pull stop, gh extension upgrade pull, then gh pull to start the new version. Also restart after switching GitHub accounts or changing token environment variables. Stop before uninstalling with gh extension remove pull.

Release builds target Linux and macOS (Intel/AMD and ARM64), and Windows x64. Private instance-control state is stored under the user's platform data directory (~/.local/state/gh-pull on Linux, ~/Library/Application Support/gh-pull on macOS, or %LOCALAPPDATA%\gh-pull on Windows). It contains a local control token, not your GitHub token. GH_PULL_STATE_DIR can override this directory for testing or isolated instances.

Requires Node.js 22+, plus either GitHub CLI authentication or a personal access token. No npm dependencies or build step are needed to run the app.

Open http://localhost:3000. Local mode is the default (AUTH_MODE=local). The server uses your GitHub CLI credentials, or GH_TOKEN / GITHUB_TOKEN if supplied. It binds only to 127.0.0.1; credentials stay on the server.

npm start and npm run dev restart the server when backend files change. Reload the browser after frontend edits. Use node server.js to run without automatic restarts.

Credentials stay in the local backend and are never sent to the browser. Both options bind only to 127.0.0.1. The extension uses --port, not the source server's PORT environment variable.

npm start reads environment variables from your shell. If you prefer a .env file, use node --env-file=.env server.js; .env files are ignored by Git.

The default query is is:open involves:@me sort:updated-desc. The server always adds is:pr; type qualifiers cannot be specified in the editor. Add qualifiers such as repo:owner/repository, author:octocat, -label:wip, or label:"good first issue", and press Enter or Search. Free text follows GitHub's search semantics (title, body, and comments by default); it no longer filters just the loaded rows.

Type a qualifier or press Ctrl+Space for suggestions. Use arrow keys to choose, Enter or Tab to accept, and Escape to dismiss. When a suggestion is selected, Enter accepts it; press Enter again to search. Repository, user, branch, and label suggestions come from loaded PRs, and you can type values that aren't suggested.

Changing Show, State, or Sort rewrites that part of the query and searches immediately. A dropdown shows Custom when the query doesn't match one of its presets. Show replaces author/involvement/review-request qualifiers; State replaces state/draft qualifiers; unrelated terms stay intact. Closed means closed and unmerged. Group by only changes presentation.

Unsubmitted edits stay in the editor while automatic refresh and pagination use the last applied query. Only applied queries are saved in the URL. Qualifiers, exclusions, and quoted phrases are supported; Boolean operators and parenthesized groups are not yet supported. Named saved queries are not implemented yet.

Actions apply to your own PRs and require GitHub write permissions:

If GitHub is still calculating mergeability, the dashboard rechecks in the background every two seconds, up to five times, without resetting loaded pages. The regular one-minute refresh continues afterward.

PRs load in pages of 50, with a 30-second server cache keyed by query and cursor. Manual and automatic refresh bypass the cache and reset pagination on success. Searches run against GitHub; grouping applies to loaded pages. All dashboard searches, including Created by me, expose at most 1,000 matches, with a notice when that limit applies. Narrow the query by repository or date to find more specific results.

Labels include the first ten per PR. Reviewers include up to 100 review requests and 100 latest reviews, with a GitHub link when more exist. Check status and counts describe the latest commit's check runs and commit statuses.

Browser storage holds name colors and account-specific viewed PR IDs/timestamps, not PR contents or credentials. Without browser storage, tracking lasts only for the current page. Reading PRs directly on GitHub does not mark them as viewed here.

PR results are cached in memory by the local process and cleared when it stops. With the extension, closing the browser leaves the process running; use gh pull stop to end it. Automatic refresh runs in the browser, so closing the dashboard stops its polling.

See the Privacy Policy, Third-party services, and Transparency disclosures for further details on data handling and security.

Tests use Node's built-in test runner and mocked GitHub responses. They cover PR behavior, CLI lifecycle and control access, authentication, and request validation using local fixture servers and mocked responses, without real GitHub credentials.

Browser interaction tests use Playwright with isolated fixture PRs. They cover editing, draft/ready changes, merges, read tracking, clipboard feedback, query autocomplete and keyboard editing, synchronized presets, pagination, stale responses, background refresh, and light/dark mobile layouts. All mutations stay in the fixture server; external browser requests are blocked.

To use an existing Chrome installation instead, set CHROME_BIN to its executable path when running npm run test:browser. Browser screenshots are written to /tmp/gh-pull-query-browser (override with BROWSER_ARTIFACT_DIR).

Our editor integration lives in public/query-editor.js; the shared query model lives in public/query.js. Both are ordinary source files and can be edited without rebuilding. Generated third-party code and its license notices live separately in public/vendor/.

Shared colors and sizing live in public/theme.css, dashboard and reusable component styles in public/style.css, and query editor styles in public/query-editor.css. Use the shared theme variables when adding UI components so light and dark modes stay consistent.

After updating CodeMirror dependencies or the exported APIs in scripts/vendor/codemirror.js, run npm run build:vendor and commit the generated files. CodeMirror, esbuild, and Playwright are development dependencies; running the server does not require installing them. The editor and vendor bundle load when the dashboard starts.

Run npm ci and npm run cli -- --no-open to try the launcher from source. Use npm run cli -- stop to stop it.

npm run build:extension builds a native standalone executable into dist/, embedding the UI, backend, Node runtime, and license notices. It uses Node's single-executable application support, esbuild, and postject; use Node 24.18.0 to match CI. The build fetches the matching Node license and leaves generated intermediates in .build/. npm run test:extension checks the actual binary and local GitHub CLI installation with isolated state and fake credentials. npm run test:extension:browser checks its browser UI on Linux using Playwright and fixture responses.

The extension workflow tests native builds on each supported platform. Version tags (v*) publish the tested binaries as GitHub release assets; pull requests only build and test artifacts. Published binaries are available on the Releases page.
