title: Kev
description: The VP of Engineering at Cognition, the applied AI lab behind Devin. Building the future of software engineering with AI.
fullText:
Pooling can hide overconfidence on one dataset and underconfidence on another, so I report both pooled and per-dataset calibration error.

To test how many questions could clear a confidence threshold, I chose a threshold for each model targeting 5% error on development data, then applied it unchanged to test. Kev-27B accepted 54% of questions with 5.5% observed error; Kev-9B accepted 36% with 6.7% error. Kev-4B accepted 31% with 3.5% error, and Kev-0.8B 15% with 5.4% error.

Those error rates won't necessarily hold on your data. Choose a threshold using representative examples, then measure it on a separate sample. Below the threshold, your code can call a larger model, retain a default, or decline the action.

To adjust the probabilities after training, I fit a temperature, a single scaling factor applied to the option scores before they're converted to probabilities. It changes confidence without changing which answer ranks first. For the new 27B and 9B, that factor is fitted on held-out datasets excluded from fine-tuning and ships with the checkpoint.

The results come from my own harness, not an independent leaderboard. The family table identifies test and development panels. Development results guided the training recipes, and earlier candidates' test results were known before I selected the released 27B, so selection was not fully blind. Qwen's training data is not fully known either; excluding a task from Kev's fine-tuning doesn't rule out exposure in the base model. Uncertainty intervals describe variation across evaluation records, not repeated training runs.

Policy and rule labels are computed by code; developer-tool labels come from human annotations, heuristics, or construction. The complaints are real CFPB narratives with model-assisted label checks. In a 50-example spot check, I agreed with 47 labels. The model cards link the measurements, label audits, and selection history.

During Kev-4B's development, one pass over 5,219 labelled consumer complaints improved accuracy from 80% to 90% on held-out complaints. On a separate example support workload, about 1,000 generated examples improved accuracy from 68% to 74%. Those are workload-specific results; a few hundred examples can produce a gain too small to distinguish from noise.

I packaged that workflow into an official kev-finetune skill. Your coding agent helps define the questions, prepares labelled data or generates examples, fine-tunes a released Kev, fits its temperature on a separate calibration split, and compares the result with the starting checkpoint before deployment.

The companion kev-deploy skill makes it easy to deploy Kev to Modal behind an authenticated HTTPS endpoint. Both skills work with Claude Code, Codex, Devin, and other coding agents. You don't need a local GPU or a clone of the Kev repository.

A small Kev-4B fine-tuning run costs about $1 in GPU time, excluding data generation and evaluation. Serving scales to zero when idle; the trade-off is a cold start, about 35 seconds in the measured setup.

Kev only scores the options you supply. It doesn't generate explanations or retrieve missing facts. You need to supply the relevant policy or evidence and handle the possibility that none of the options is correct. Answer order can also shift probabilities slightly.

Kev-27B was trained on documents up to 32k tokens and evaluated up to 64k. It runs on a single H100 for shorter inputs, but the measured 64k-token case used more than 80 GB of memory and needs an H200 or B200. The smaller Kevs were trained on documents up to about 7,500 tokens.

The code, weights, and evaluation reports are available, but the full 27B training corpus and some evaluation data are private. The model cards document what others can reproduce.

The weights are on Hugging Face, and the code, model cards, and serving instructions are on GitHub. You can try Kev-4B in your browser before setting anything up.

Install the skills, then ask your coding agent to “deploy Kev-4B” or “fine-tune Kev on my support tickets”:

title: Sorry we made you grind LeetCode
description: A note from Vivek, HackerRank's co-founder and CEO, on why technical hiring has to change in the agentic era.
fullText:
I’m Vivek, co-founder/ceo of HackerRank. We’re sorry we made you grind leetcode. That line is on billboards around SF now.

HackerRank didn’t invent algorithmic interviews, but we helped normalize a version of technical hiring that turned into months of grinding questions with little connection to the actual job.

Technical interviews have come a long way: from “How many golf balls fit in a 747?” to reading code over the phone, writing it on a whiteboard, and eventually solving LeetCode-style problems.

Each step got us a little closer to the work. But we were still mostly evaluating how well someone had prepared for an interview, not how well they could build software.

Developers increasingly plan with agents, build with them, and review their output. They need to know when the code is good, when it needs another pass, and when it’s completely wrong.

The hiring process needs to evolve too.

At HackerRank, we’re changing three things:

We’ve packaged this into Chakra, our agentic interviewer.

Candidates get a realistic problem and access to AI tools. They solve it as they would in the real world. Chakra then digs deeper: Why did you choose that approach? What would you change? How did you validate the AI-generated code?

You can now see how well someone solved the problem and not just the output.

Do algorithm questions still have value? Yes, they do but the problem is the weightage associated with them.

title: Pizza in North Korea
fullText:
North Korea has several restaurants serving pizza.[a] Most people in the country cannot afford pizza, and it is mostly available for the elite. Pyongyang has five restaurants that serve pizza, including Pizza Restaurant on Kwangbok Street [ko] and Italy Pizza on Mirae Scientists Street. Kim Jong Il hired Italian chefs to train North Koreans in pizza making and introduced it to the country.

North Korean leader Kim Jong Il, who was noted for his lavish culinary habits, made efforts to introduce international cuisine in the 1990s.[2] In the spring of 1997, he had pizzaiolo Ermanno Furlanis flown into Pyongyang, along with another Italian chef and both of their wives, to train North Korean chefs in pizza-making for three weeks.[2][3] The Italian chefs brought two pizza ovens, which were allegedly intercepted by CIA agents at the Berlin airport.[3]

Furlanis described his experience in a three-part series for Asia Times Online in August 2001.[2] He wrote that he was subjected to an extensive medical examination and tests of his cooking skill before he could begin instruction, and noted that his pupils measured the distance between olives. "I could not explain the concept of creativity", he noted.[2]

All day I was only expected to prepare 10 or 20 pizzas, and this usually took me no more than a couple of hours. My pupils gravely noted down the most trivial details and gradually began doing much of the work themselves, picking up my techniques with amazing rapidity.

In 2008, North Korean chefs were sent to Naples and Rome for training in Italian pizza and pasta. Kim did not authorize the opening of the country's first pizzeria until December 2008,[4] after chefs had mastered pizza preparation with "repeated trial and error", as reported by Choson Sinbo, a North Korea-aligned newspaper published in Japan.[5]

The restaurant, called Pizza Restaurant,[b] opened on Kwangbok Street [ko]. Its chefs used flour, butter, and cheese that had been flown in from Italy, as well as an Italian pizza oven.[5][7][8][9] Pizza Restaurant was managed by Kim Sang-Soon, who said Kim believed "the people should also be allowed access to the world's famous dishes".[7]

According to Choson Sinbo, Pizza Restaurant was busy in the months following its opening, and provided many of its customers with their first Italian meals.[4] Its menu in 2010 included 11 traditional pizzas, though Italian food comprised only two-fifths of the menu. The Korea Times called it "Pyongyang's best pizzeria".[1] Lonely Planet listed it as "pretty decent".[10]

In response to publicity about Pizza Restaurant, London-based South Korean artist Kim Hwang created a short film series, "Pizzas for the People". After filming in South Korea and premiering at a festival in Heidelberg, the series was burned onto 500 DVDs, which five smugglers brought across the border into North Korea.[10][8] The series satirizes the exclusivity of pizza in North Korea and combines elements of a cooking show and mockumentary.[8][10][9] It presents aspects of Western democracy, and demonstrates how to make potato dough pizza with tofu instead of cheese and a liquor bottle as a rolling pin.[11][8] Kim Hwang's smugglers brought back fan mail from viewers, but he did not know how many North Koreans the film series reached.[9]

According to travel writer Jamie Fullerton, Pyolmuri Café, a European-style café that opened with funding from the Adventist Development and Relief Agency, was the first restaurant in Pyongyang to serve pizza.[6][8]

In 2011, a new pizzeria owned by Corital, an Italian–North Korean joint venture, was reported to serve Coca-Cola. Coca-Cola said it did not authorize the sale of the product, which would violate United States sanctions against North Korea.[12][13]

The third Italian restaurant in Pyongyang, Italy Pizza, opened in late 2015 as part of the launch of Mirae Scientists Street.[14] It serves less traditional pizza than the Kwangbok Street pizzeria. Its staff performs live music twice a day.[1] Vice described its decor as "1970s cruise liner-level kitsch" and its pizza as "pretty good" despite being served without cheese.[14] The restaurant existed before the redevelopment of Mirae Street, when the building was replaced with another at the same location.[15]

As of 2021[update], Pyongyang has five restaurants that serve pizza.[15] It has more Italian restaurants than Chinese restaurants.[6] North Korean street markets, a major source of food, sell pepperoni pizza for wealthy customers.[16] North Korean foreign propaganda videos, such as the Echo of Truth YouTube series, have shown pizzerias.[17][18]

In 2018, a pizza cost about US$5 to US$10 ($6 to $13 in 2025), which most North Koreans cannot afford. Pizza is eaten by Pyongyang elites, diplomats, and foreigners.[8] A pizza may cost a month's salary for a middle-ranking official.[19] Since middle- and upper-class individuals are allowed to live in cities, Western-style restaurants have become popular in Pyongyang.[14]

Restaurants serve pizza with traditional toppings, as well as local varieties like kimchi pizza. All restaurants, including pizzerias, serve familiar dishes in North Korean cuisine. Most customers order these rather than pizza.[15]

fullText:
Kanishka Narayan to say Britain cannot rely entirely on tech companies amid rising global concern over AI dangers

Companies building the most advanced AI systems must increase safety efforts, the UK’s AI minister will say, as he announces a strengthening of Britain’s cyber defences.

Kanishka Narayan will call on companies developing frontier AI to do more to make sure it is safe. He will say Britain cannot rely entirely on technology companies to police their own models and will argue the UK needs to build more of its own AI infrastructure.

Narayan’s speech in west London will be the first since Andy Burnham made AI a cabinet-level brief. It comes as Geoffrey Irving, a former chief scientist at the UK’s AI Security Institute, which tests the most powerful AI models, raised fears enemy states could steal unreleased cutting-edge models. Amid increasing global concern at dangers posed by AI, Irving told the Guardian: “The AI companies do not have security that would prevent an adversarial country from stealing the models.”

He cited a recent incident at OpenAI where it was “hacked” by cybersecurity researchers, who said “the scope of what we could theoretically access was huge”. The attack was carried out under an OpenAI programme that rewarded ethical hackers testing its systems. OpenAI says it has multiple protections against theft of its models, including encryption and continuous monitoring.

Irving, a former employee at OpenAI and Google DeepMind who now runs an AI safety research body, has warned there is a “50% chance” of humanity being wiped out by superintelligent AIs and the only answer, for now, is to stop development of advanced systems as soon as possible. Irving is concerned by the rate of progress in alarming attributes shown by models, which could lead to them becoming highly advanced in traits such as concealing their actions and manipulating humans.

“It is possible we [will] get superintelligence in less than 12 months, on the current path,” he said.

Narayan’s speech will be watched closely for signs the UK may join a call for international governments to coordinate common safety standards for AIs, which has been signed by leaders of nations including Finland, France, Germany, Australia, Singapore, the UAE and Ireland, but not the UK and the US, where Donald Trump has said he wants the leading AI companies to “self-police”. The international alliance calling for strict rules comes after a wave of recent incidents with misaligned advanced AIs hacking into private and government systems.

In one of the latest cases, Anthropic on Friday revealed that when it was testing a version of its Claude model the AI contacted police claiming it could help solve a murder. It had landed on a page containing a police department tip form and a mention of an unsolved homicide. It wrote: “I may have information regarding this case. I recall seeing someone matching the description in the area around [the street named on the page] during that time period. Please contact me if this information is relevant.” Although Claude was instructed never to log in, create accounts, enter personal data, make purchases, or submit anything destructive, its instructions did not rule out form submissions.

Last week UK intelligence leaders from MI5, MI6 and GCHQ briefed the cabinet on AI’s threat to national security, according to the Sunday Times. The warning from the spy chiefs is being seen by some as encouragement for Burnham to grip the AI safety issue more firmly.

The prime minister told the UN last month that Britain would use its G20 presidency next year to champion agreement on AI safety with “a single set of global principles and standards”. But safety experts are calling for faster action to avert the most serious risks, which range from advanced AIs being used to mount a cyber-attack on essential infrastructure to the creation of novel bioweapons.

Meanwhile, Satya Nadella, the chair and chief executive of Microsoft, which operates AI infrastructure and is an OpenAI shareholder, on Saturday called for AI models to be designed with an “emergency brake”. He said people needed to start from the principle of assuming advanced AI models posed an insider risk.

“We can’t treat Super Intelligence as a set of nested black boxes and simply accept or reject its recommendations, answers, and actions,” he wrote. “We must build contained systems whose behaviour we can observe, limits we can test, and actions we can always contain.”

fullText:
LONDON, Oct 11 (Reuters) - British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Russia interfered in the 2016 Brexit vote, as he warned voters in France and ‌Germany about Moscow-backed efforts to influence their politics.

Burnham, who took over as Britain's ‌leader in July and said last month that Britain could consider rejoining the European Union in the future, ​is the first British prime minister to say openly there was evidence of Russian interference in the referendum a decade ago.

"I asked the question coming to Downing Street, was there interference in the 2016 referendum from Russia? And I've had the clear answer that yes, there was," Burnham ‌said in an interview with ⁠The Rest Is Politics podcast released on Sunday.

Burnham did not spell out how he believed that Russia interfered in the referendum and gave no ⁠details on what evidence this statement was based.

The Russian embassy in London did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Russia has previously denied meddling in the Brexit vote, casting Britain as ​gripped by ​anti-Russian hysteria.

Burnham's comments mark a departure from those ​of former Prime Minister Boris Johnson, ‌who campaigned to leave the EU, and said in 2020 there was no evidence of Russian interference in the referendum.

Britons voted 52%-48% to leave the EU in 2016, plunging the country into its biggest political crisis since World War Two.

Burnham said voters in European democracies needed to be better informed about efforts to disrupt their politics.

"I mean, these things are ‌important now to put clearly on the record, and ​I believe, help voters in Germany and France understand ​that some of this politics is ​instigated via our enemies, namely Russia," he said.

Britain's government failed to establish ‌whether Russia meddled in the 2016 referendum ​on membership of the ​EU, according to a report by parliament's Intelligence and Security Committee in 2020.

The report also found that Russia had sought to influence Scotland's 2014 independence referendum, in which ​voters rejected independence.

Burnham last month ‌said he could campaign to take Britain back into the EU at the ​next general election, reopening the country's divisive debate on its relationship with ​the continent.

title: Sheff Utd legend Sharp retires after 22-year career
description: Sheffield United legend Billy Sharp announces his retirement from football at the age of 40.
fullText:
Sheffield United legend Billy Sharp has announced his retirement from football at the age of 40.

Sharp, who played for Southampton, Nottingham Forest, Leeds United, Hull City, Scunthorpe United, Reading, Doncaster Rovers and Rushden & Diamonds during a 22-year professional career, during which he scored 299 goals.

He had been a free agent since leaving Doncaster at the end of last season, when he signed off in style in his final game with a hat-trick against Peterborough.

"I'm going to hang my boots up. I've given it a good ride. I've got a long way, got to 40," Sharp told Sky Sports.

"I wanted to go out on my own terms. I've seen many friends get taken away by injury and things like that.

"I wanted to go out with a bang and luckily for me, I got a hat-trick in my last appearance.

"I'm maybe not the most talented player, maybe not the most liked on the pitch but that's because I love football. I'm passionate and I think I've got every single bit out of my career.

"I've made memories in football that will last me a lifetime."

A boyhood Blades supporter, Sharp made his Championship debut off the bench against Watford in November 2004.

He went on to become club captain and an important figure in three promotion-winning campaigns - from League One in 2017 and the Championship in 2019 and 2023.

In three spells with Sheffield United, Sharp scored 129 goals for the club and became a Blades icon.

He was also part of the Southampton side that won promotion to the Premier League in 2012.

He enjoyed a brief stay in the MLS with LA Galaxy in 2023, after which many thought retirement loomed - but the ageless Sharp returned to his native Yorkshire to extend his career, firstly with Hull and then Doncaster Rovers.

Sharp scored a dramatic late winner against Bradford City to secure promotion to League One for Rovers in 2025 before his spectacular ending to last season which meant he had scored EFL hat-tricks in his teens, 20s, 30s and 40s. He did score a fourth against Peterborough which would have taken him to 300 career goals but it was ruled out for offside.

"It would have been lovely to have got that 300th goal on that day but I've had an unbelievable career," he said.

Sharp has joined Baller League team N5, which is led by former Arsenal and Germany goalkeeper Jens Lehmann to play six-a-side football but he also has one eye on management having completed his coaching badges.

title: South African Simons to join England Test set-up
description: England are set to add the first name to Stephen Fleming’s backroom team, with Eric Simons joining as Test bowling coach.
fullText:
England are set to add the first name to Stephen Fleming's backroom team, with Eric Simons joining as Test bowling coach.

Former South Africa head coach Simons is a long-time ally of Fleming, having worked alongside him in the Indian Premier League (IPL) with Chennai Super Kings.

Simons' new role will be confirmed on Monday, when England announce the latest round of central contracts.

New Zealander Fleming is assembling a backroom team for his first series in charge, against South Africa in December.

The shake-up in the staff comes as England once again split head-coaching responsibilities across formats. Fleming is in charge of the Test side and Brendon McCullum leads the white-ball teams.

When McCullum was Test coach, England used a number of fast-bowling consultants, including James Anderson, David Saker and Tim Southee.

Saker will be part of the England staff for the one-day tri-series in Pakistan this month, alongside long-term McCullum assistant Jeetan Patel, Mike Yardy and Carl Hopkinson.

Southee and fielding coach Sarah Taylor, who have been with England throughout the home summer, might rejoin the team later in the winter.

Kevin Pietersen has been appointed as a batting consultant to the white-ball teams in the run-up to the 50-over World Cup in southern Africa.

Former England batter Pietersen will not be on the tour of Pakistan, but is due to join the squad for the white-ball tour of Australia and then in South Africa for the three one-day internationals in the country of his birth in January.

Marcus Trescothick took interim charge of the Test team for the series against Pakistan. His future in the England set-up has been the subject of speculation and is yet to be confirmed.

Simons, 64, played 23 one-day internationals for South Africa in 1994 and 1995.

He also worked with Fleming at the Joburg Super Kings in the SA20 and the Texas Super Kings in Major League Cricket.

Simons had two years in charge of the South Africa team between 2002 and 2004 and a spell as India's bowling coach.

fullText:
Oct 11 (Reuters) - A US judge on Sunday blocked the Trump administration from using taxpayer money to pay for political advertisements, after ‌publicly funded television ads glorifying US President Donald Trump began airing in ‌late September and sparked a bipartisan backlash.

Manhattan-based US District Judge Jennifer Rochon temporarily barred the advertisements after ​plaintiffs including watchdog group Common Cause brought a lawsuit alleging the ads were political propaganda designed to help Republican candidates in the November 3 midterm elections, not public service announcements.

The Trump administration was already planning to stop running the ads before Rochon's order, ‌according to a separate statement ⁠filed with the court on Saturday.

The decision caps days of controversy over the taxpayer-funded advertisements, which were aired in the final weeks ⁠before the midterm elections.

"We won't stop until this administration is held fully accountable, and no president from any party can waste and abuse taxpayer funds for propaganda ever again," said ​Common ​Cause President and CEO Virginia Kase Solomón.

Trump on ​Monday said he considered the ‌ads to be a "positive promotion for our great U.S.A." but that they would no longer be funded by taxpayers, and the White House said this week that the president's political action committee, MAGA PAC, would fund the ads going forward.

The White House said Trump's political action committee will not reimburse taxpayers for the ads that have already ‌run. The ads end with a disclaimer saying they ​were paid for by the US government. The ​Justice Department did not immediately respond ​to a request for comment about the judge's order.

The plaintiffs, which ‌also included a public employee union ​and a candidate for ​Alabama state representative, had asked Rochon to temporarily block the ads by Friday so that they could not air during weekend programming such as football games and ​Saturday Night Live.

Democratic Party ‌officials also challenged the ads in a separate suit brought in federal court ​in Washington.

Shortly before Trump’s declaration, Zelenskyy told Jon Karl on "This Week" that Ukraine wanted an immediate "energy ceasefire" that would see it stop striking Russian oil refineries provided the Kremlin halted attacks on Ukraine’s power infrastructure.

fullText:
PENSACOLA, Fla. (AP) — People in the Florida Panhandle and southern Alabama cleaned up after Hurricane Isaias swept through as the storm's remnants caused flooding in North Carolina on Sunday, while powerful Pacific Ocean waves stirred up by Rachel, a former tropical storm, battered the coast of Southern California.

In western North Carolina, rivers overflowed as heavy rainfall raised the risk of flash and urban flooding, according to the National Weather Service. It said tornadoes were possible in parts of Virginia and North Carolina as well as dangerous surf and rip current conditions along the Gulf and southeastern Atlantic coasts.

At least four deaths were linked to Isaias, the first hurricane of the Atlantic season, which came ashore as a Category 2 hurricane Friday near Destin, Florida, a Gulf Coast vacation spot filled with high-rises and tourist shops. The storm then roared into Alabama with tropical-force winds before heading farther north.

In Florida's Escambia County, Sheriff Chip Simmons said a woman was killed when a tree fell on her home and a man died of carbon monoxide fumes from a generator running in his garage.

One person died when a tree fell on a house in Birmingham, said Cory Moon, the city's fire chief. A second storm-related death in Alabama was attributed to a motor vehicle crash involving a downed tree in Barbour County, said Josh Johnson of the state's emergency management agency.

In Burke County, North Carolina, an unhoused male and female were camping when floodwaters from the Catawba River caught them off guard. They were rescued, along with their dog, according to a spokesperson for the county emergency management agency. Separately, a woman trapped inside her car in floodwaters was freed outside of Morganton.

In McDowell County, North Carolina, just west of Burke County, first responders said they dealt with five landslides and voluntary evacuations overnight Saturday into Sunday as they responded to flooded roads and streams overflowing their banks.

Nearly a dozen local weather stations in the western North Carolina county reported torrential 24-hour rainfall totals from about 5 inches (13 centimeters) to as much as 9.57 inches (24 centimeters) at the fire/rescue station in Enola. The weather service said rainfall was diminishing in the area but that rapid river rises and flooding remained possible.

Hurricane-force winds in the Florida Panhandle blew the roof off a Pensacola hotel. The storm flattened a boathouse in Destin and ripped away part of the facade of a high-rise in Panama City Beach.

At a church in Pensacola where the United Cajun Navy was distributing supplies Sunday morning, a line of hundreds of cars stretched around the block. Yvette Haro said she arrived at 5 a.m. after being turned away the previous day because supplies had run out.

With a 10-year-old son and a 5-year-old daughter at home, she said it's hard to go to stores and wait in long lines. She was looking for water, paper towels, toilet paper and cleaning supplies.

While her home didn't suffer any damage, the loss of electricity was making things difficult, Haro said. "The biggest thing is our food going bad," she said.

About 226,000 customers remained without power Sunday evening in the Florida Panhandle and southern Alabama, according to poweroutage.com. Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said he expected nearly everyone to have it restored by Tuesday night.

Rachel became a post-tropical cyclone overnight, bringing unusually big waves to Southern California.

Waves battered a century-old wooden boardwalk on the Long Beach peninsula and forced homeowners to evacuate. The strip of multimillion-dollar oceanfront properties, along with much of the Southern California coastline, was already reeling from Hurricane Marie in September.

"This area is completely shattered and vulnerable," Jack Gordon, a Long Beach real estate agent, said.

The Pacific Ocean is abnormally warm, about 7 to 8 degrees F warmer than normal for this time of year, due to the El Niño weather pattern, said Joe Sirard of the weather service in Oxnard, California

"When we have this warm water, it actually causes the ocean to rise above the normal predicted tide levels," Sirard said. That's affected by Rachel's ocean swells and wind gusts. The City of Long Beach placed dozens of 3,000-pound (1,360-kilogram) sandbags along the stretch of peninsula where waves tore apart the historic boardwalk and smashed against coastal homes.

Jazmin Evers, a 37-year-old mother who runs a pottery business from her Long Beach rental home, said the community is on edge. "Every time the tide goes down everyone just kind of takes a breath — except, of course, the people whose buildings are being destroyed," she said. "When the tide comes back up, everybody's nerves kind of ramp back up." Rachel dissipated over Las Vegas as it drenched deserts across the Southwest. An inch (2.4 centimeters) of rain fell in the city Sunday, leading to gushing water and flooded streets on the Las Vegas Strip.

In the Pacific, Hurricane Simon was a Category 4 storm as it pounded Mexico's Pacific coast Sunday, its eye remaining just offshore as its most powerful winds and rain slammed people living between the Sierra Madre and the ocean. ___

Brumback reported from Atlanta. Walker reported from New York. Kathy McCormack in Concord, New Hampshire, Jack Brook in New Orleans and Josh Kelety in Phoenix also contributed.

fullText:
A businessman wanted for years in the U.S. for allegedly paying bribes to top Venezuelan officials in exchange for lucrative state contracts in Venezuela has been taken into custody.

Alvaro Pulido was indicted in Miami federal court in 2019 and again in 2021 as part of an investigation into his longtime business partner, Alex Saab, a one-time ally of ousted President Nicolás Maduro. The U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration and State Department had been offering a reward of up to $10 million for information leading to his arrest.

Pulido was taken into U.S. custody after an investigation led by the DEA, FBI and Homeland Security Investigations agencies, Nicole Navas Oxman, a Homeland Security Task Force spokesperson, said Sunday.

Oxman didn't say how Pulido ended up in U.S. custody but said he will make his initial court appearance Tuesday in Miami.

Venezuelan authorities have so far been silent about the arrest, reflecting the challenge acting President Delcy Rodríguez faces in appeasing elements of the ruling coalition that want her to resist attempts by the Trump administration to round up scores of Venezuelan insiders wanted by the U.S., sometimes for years, for serious crimes ranging from corruption to drug trafficking.

The Colombian-born Pulido was arrested in Venezuela in 2023 as part of a sprawling crackdown on corruption inside state-run oil company PDVSA that was led by Rodríguez while she was serving as Maduro's vice president. She took over as Venezuela's acting president following the U.S. military's ouster of Maduro in January.

Prosecutors allege that Pulido, together with Saab, created a network of offshore shell companies to funnel bribes to top Maduro allies in exchange for contracts to import food, medicine and low-cost housing at a time of widespread hardship in the South American country.

Saab, who also hails from Colombia, was deported to the U.S. by Rodríguez in May. Last month, he pleaded guilty in a related bribery case, agreeing to cooperate against Maduro and other individuals and forfeit $195 million in criminal proceeds from the corruption scheme.
